s:
A. On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can remain several degrees warmer than the farmland around it. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island, arises largely because asphalt, brick and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly after sunset. Tall buildings compound the problem by trapping that heat and blocking the breezes that might otherwise carry it away.
B. The consequences extend well beyond discomfort. Warm nights deny the body the chance to recover from daytime heat, and public health researchers have linked prolonged heatwaves in dense neighbourhoods to increased hospital admissions, particularly among elderly residents. Demand for air conditioning also rises, which in turn releases more waste heat into the streets, a cycle that is difficult to interrupt.
C. Among the remedies proposed, green roofs have attracted particular attention. A layer of soil and vegetation shields the roof from direct sunlight, while water evaporating from leaves draws heat from the surrounding air. Some studies suggest that buildings fitted with such roofs need noticeably less energy for cooling, although the benefit varies with climate, building height and the plants chosen.
D. Critics, however, caution against treating green roofs as a universal solution. Installation is costly, older structures may not support the weight of saturated soil, and in arid regions the irrigation needed to keep plants alive can strain scarce water supplies. Moreover, a garden on a twenty-storey tower does little to cool the pavement where pedestrians actually walk.
E. For this reason, many planners now favour a combined approach. Reflective paving, street trees and well-placed parks can each lower temperatures at ground level, and their effects appear greatest when they are spread across a neighbourhood rather than concentrated in a single showcase project. The aim is not to eliminate the heat island, which may be impossible, but to make it less dangerous.

Which heading best fits paragraph D?
c: Practical limits of a popular remedy
Why green roofs fail in every climate
The health risks of rooftop gardens
How plants cool the surrounding air
a: D paragrafı yeşil çatıların maliyet, ağırlık, sulama ve yaya düzeyinde etkisizlik gibi sınırlılıklarını sıralar. 'Every climate' aşırı genellemedir; sorun yalnızca kurak bölgeler için söylenir.

s:
A. A healthy coral reef is far from silent. Snapping shrimp produce a constant crackle, fish grunt and click as they feed or defend territory, and the movement of countless small creatures adds a low background hum. Marine biologists have increasingly come to regard this chorus not as mere noise but as a source of information for the animals that hear it.
B. Many reef fish begin life as tiny larvae drifting in the open ocean, far from the habitat in which they will eventually settle. How they find their way back was long a puzzle. Experiments in which underwater speakers broadcast recorded reef sounds have indicated that the larvae of several species are drawn towards these recordings, implying that sound may act as a kind of acoustic beacon.
C. Degraded reefs, by contrast, tend to be much quieter. Where coral has been bleached or damaged, the diversity of resident animals declines, and the soundscape becomes thinner and less varied. Some researchers fear that this creates a damaging feedback loop: a reef that sounds lifeless attracts fewer young fish, and fewer fish means slower recovery.
D. This possibility has inspired a striking idea known as acoustic enrichment. In trials on damaged reef patches, loudspeakers playing the sounds of a thriving reef were installed, and in some cases more juvenile fish gathered there than at comparable silent sites. Supporters argue that the technique could complement physical restoration, such as transplanting coral fragments.
E. Others are more cautious. Playback can attract fish, they note, but it cannot provide food or shelter, and luring animals to a habitat that cannot sustain them might do more harm than good. Equipment must also be maintained in a corrosive environment. Most scientists therefore describe acoustic enrichment as a promising tool to be tested further rather than a proven method.

Which heading best fits paragraph B?
c: A possible answer to a navigational puzzle
The dangers of the open ocean for larvae
Why reef sounds are growing steadily louder
How loudspeakers harm young reef fish
a: B paragrafı larvaların resife nasıl geri döndüğü bilmecesini ve sesin bir 'akustik işaret' olabileceği açıklamasını anlatır.

s:
A. Classical economic theory assumes that the value a person places on an object should not depend on whether they happen to own it. If someone would pay a certain amount to acquire a coffee mug, they should be willing to sell the same mug for roughly the same amount. Yet laboratory studies have repeatedly found otherwise. When participants are randomly given an item and then offered the chance to sell it, they typically demand considerably more than other participants are prepared to pay for an identical item.
B. Psychologists have labelled this tendency the endowment effect. One widely cited explanation links it to loss aversion, the observation that losses tend to feel more painful than equivalent gains feel pleasant. Parting with something one owns is experienced as a loss, so a higher price is needed to compensate for it.
C. Not all researchers accept this account. Some argue that the effect is partly an artefact of experimental design: participants who misunderstand the rules may inflate their selling prices simply to avoid being exploited. When instructions are made clearer and practice rounds are provided, the gap between buying and selling prices has, in certain studies, narrowed considerably.
D. The effect also appears to vary with experience. Traders who buy and sell goods as a matter of routine seem less susceptible, perhaps because they come to view items as stock rather than as possessions. This suggests that the bias may be learned away, at least in particular settings.
E. Whatever its origin, the endowment effect has practical implications. Free trial periods, for instance, may work partly because customers begin to regard a product as their own and become reluctant to give it up when the trial ends. Marketers, it seems, have long understood intuitively what economists took decades to document.

Which title best suits the passage as a whole?
c: How traders profit from free trials
a: Parçanın tamamı, sahip olmanın bir nesneye biçilen değeri nasıl artırdığını (endowment effect), açıklamalarını ve sonuçlarını ele alır.

s:
A. Before the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Noon was simply the moment when the sun stood highest in the local sky, and because this moment shifts as one travels east or west, clocks in neighbouring towns might differ by several minutes. For communities in which few people travelled far or fast, the discrepancy caused little inconvenience.
B. The arrival of the railways changed this. A train could cover in hours a distance that had once taken days, and timetables became almost impossible to interpret when every station observed a different hour. Passengers missed connections and, more seriously, the risk of collisions on single-track lines grew when crews worked from inconsistent clocks.
C. Railway companies responded by adopting a single reference time across their networks, usually that of a major city or observatory. Telegraph lines, which often ran alongside the tracks, allowed time signals to be transmitted to distant stations so that clocks could be synchronised. Gradually, the time kept by the railways came to be used by the towns themselves.
D. The change was not universally welcomed. Some residents objected that their days were now governed by a distant authority rather than by the sun overhead, and for a period certain public clocks displayed two minute hands, one for local time and one for railway time. Legal disputes occasionally arose over which time applied to contracts or to the opening hours of public buildings.
E. Eventually, the logic of coordination prevailed, and national and later international systems of time zones were established. Today, the idea that time should be standardised seems so natural that it is easy to forget it was once a contested innovation, shaped less by astronomy than by the practical needs of transport and commerce.

Which heading best fits paragraph C?
c: Spreading a uniform time across networks
The invention of the electric telegraph
Why towns rejected railway time completely
a: C paragrafı demiryolu şirketlerinin tek bir referans saat benimseyip telgrafla bunu uzak istasyonlara yaymasını anlatır.

s:
A. Linguists estimate that a large proportion of the world's languages are spoken by relatively small communities, and many of these are no longer being learned by children. When a generation grows up speaking only a dominant regional or national language, the ancestral language may survive for a time among older speakers, but its long-term future becomes uncertain.
B. The causes of such shifts are rarely linguistic. Economic opportunity, schooling, migration to cities and the prestige attached to certain languages all encourage families to adopt the language that seems most useful for their children's prospects. In some historical cases, minority languages were actively discouraged in schools, leaving a legacy of reluctance among parents to pass them on.
C. The loss of a language is often described as a loss of knowledge. Vocabulary can encode detailed understanding of local plants, animals and landscapes, and oral traditions preserve histories that may never have been written down. Yet many advocates stress that the most important consideration is the community's own wish to maintain its identity, rather than the interests of outside researchers.
D. Revitalisation efforts take many forms. Some communities have established "language nests", in which young children spend their days with fluent elders, absorbing the language through play and routine. Others have produced dictionaries, recordings and, more recently, mobile applications. Results vary widely, and experience suggests that technology alone cannot substitute for daily use within families.
E. A language that has fallen out of everyday use is not necessarily beyond recovery. There are examples of languages that have been revived from limited documentation, although the version that emerges inevitably differs from the speech of earlier generations. Supporters argue that such change is natural, since every living language evolves.

s:
A. The rapid growth of electric vehicles has prompted a question that receives less attention than driving range or charging speed: what happens to batteries at the end of their useful life? Lithium-ion cells contain valuable materials, including lithium, cobalt and nickel, whose extraction from mines carries environmental and social costs. Recovering these materials from used batteries could, in principle, reduce the need for new mining.
B. In practice, recycling is complicated. Batteries vary considerably in size, shape and chemistry, which makes automated dismantling difficult. Cells that retain some charge can catch fire if damaged during handling, so they must usually be discharged first. Many packs are also assembled with strong adhesives, a design choice that improves durability but hinders disassembly.
C. Two broad recycling methods are currently in use. Pyrometallurgy involves smelting batteries at high temperatures; it is relatively tolerant of mixed inputs but consumes considerable energy and tends to lose some materials, lithium among them. Hydrometallurgy instead dissolves shredded material in chemical solutions, from which individual metals are recovered. It can achieve higher recovery rates but generates liquid waste that must be treated.
D. An alternative to recycling is reuse. A battery that no longer meets the demands of a vehicle may still hold enough capacity for less demanding tasks, such as storing electricity from solar panels in a building. This "second life" postpones recycling rather than replacing it, but it extracts more value from the original manufacturing effort.
E. Some engineers argue that the most effective improvements will come at the design stage. Batteries built to be taken apart easily, with standardised components and clear labelling of their chemistry, would be cheaper and safer to process. Some governments have already begun to introduce rules that encourage such practices.

Which paragraph describes a feature that is useful during one stage of a battery's life but a problem at another?
a: B paragrafındaki güçlü yapıştırıcılar dayanıklılığı artırır ama sökmeyi zorlaştırır; yani kullanımda yararlı, geri dönüşümde sorunludur.

s:
A. Few activities in the art world provoke as much argument as the restoration of old paintings. Over centuries, varnish yellows, pigments fade and earlier repairs discolour, so that a work may look quite different from the way it appeared when it left the artist's studio. Restorers aim to stabilise the object and, often, to recover something of its original appearance.
B. The difficulty lies in deciding what "original" means. Removing darkened varnish can reveal bright colours that surprise viewers accustomed to a sombre surface. Critics sometimes protest that a cleaned painting looks harsh or flat, arguing that the artist may have applied thin final layers, known as glazes, which aggressive cleaning could remove along with the dirt.
C. Modern conservation is guided by several principles intended to limit such risks. One is reversibility: any material added by a restorer should be removable in future without harming the original paint. Another is documentation, so that later specialists know exactly what has been done. Analytical techniques such as infrared imaging and microscopic sampling also allow conservators to examine paint layers before intervening.
D. Even so, the question of how much to repair remains open. Where areas of paint have been lost, some conservators fill the gaps in a way that blends invisibly with the surrounding surface; others prefer retouching that looks seamless from a distance but can be identified on close inspection. The second approach reflects a belief that viewers deserve to know which parts are authentic.
E. Ultimately, restoration involves judgement as well as science. Each decision reflects assumptions about the artist's intentions, the expectations of the public and the responsibilities owed to future generations, and these assumptions may themselves change over time. A treatment that seems restrained today may appear heavy-handed to the next generation of conservators.

c: Differing views on how visible repairs should be

The public's demand for invisible repairs
a: D paragrafı kayıp boya alanlarının görünmez biçimde mi yoksa yakından fark edilebilir biçimde mi doldurulacağına ilişkin iki yaklaşımı karşılaştırır.

s:
A. Few activities in the art world provoke as much argument as the restoration of old paintings. Over centuries, varnish yellows, pigments fade and earlier repairs discolour, so that a work may look quite different from the way it appeared when it left the artist's studio. Restorers aim to stabilise the object and, often, to recover something of its original appearance.
B. The difficulty lies in deciding what "original" means. Removing darkened varnish can reveal bright colours that surprise viewers accustomed to a sombre surface. Critics sometimes protest that a cleaned painting looks harsh or flat, arguing that the artist may have applied thin final layers, known as glazes, which aggressive cleaning could remove along with the dirt.
C. Modern conservation is guided by several principles intended to limit such risks. One is reversibility: any material added by a restorer should be removable in future without harming the original paint. Another is documentation, so that later specialists know exactly what has been done. Analytical techniques such as infrared imaging and microscopic sampling also allow conservators to examine paint layers before intervening.
D. Even so, the question of how much to repair remains open. Where areas of paint have been lost, some conservators fill the gaps in a way that blends invisibly with the surrounding surface; others prefer retouching that looks seamless from a distance but can be identified on close inspection. The second approach reflects a belief that viewers deserve to know which parts are authentic.
E. Ultimately, restoration involves judgement as well as science. Each decision reflects assumptions about the artist's intentions, the expectations of the public and the responsibilities owed to future generations, and these assumptions may themselves change over time. A treatment that seems restrained today may appear heavy-handed to the next generation of conservators.

A. Until the middle of the twentieth century, sleep was widely regarded as a passive state in which the brain simply rested. Research since then has challenged this view. Recordings of brain activity show that sleep consists of distinct stages that recur in cycles throughout the night, each characterised by different patterns of electrical activity.
B. A growing body of evidence suggests that some of these stages contribute to memory. In a typical experiment, participants learn a list of word pairs or a motor task, such as a sequence of finger movements, and are tested later after either a period of sleep or an equivalent period awake. Those who have slept frequently perform better, even when the time elapsed is the same.
C. One influential theory proposes that during deep sleep the brain replays patterns of activity associated with recent experiences. According to this account, the replay gradually transfers information from the hippocampus, a region involved in forming new memories, to the cortex, where it can be stored for the longer term. Studies in rodents have reported replay of activity sequences first recorded while the animals were running through mazes.
D. Not every finding fits neatly into this picture. The size of the sleep benefit differs between types of memory and between studies, and some researchers argue that sleep may help chiefly by protecting new memories from interference rather than by actively strengthening them. During waking hours, after all, the brain is constantly absorbing new information that could disrupt what was recently learned.
E. These debates have practical relevance. Students who sacrifice sleep to study late may undermine the very learning they hope to secure. Nonetheless, scientists generally caution against simple claims that particular sleep routines will dramatically improve memory, since much remains to be understood.

Why the brain rests completely during the night

When city planners first proposed painting rooftops white to reflect sunlight, critics dismissed the idea as too modest to matter. s:
Text 1
Some preservationists insist that a historic building should be restored to its original condition, down to the paint colors and window frames. Any modern alteration, they argue, erases evidence of how people in the past actually lived and built, leaving later generations with a structure that is historic in name only.

Text 2
Advocates of adaptive reuse counter that a building no one can use is unlikely to survive at all. Converting an old textile mill into apartments may require new windows and wiring, but it gives owners an economic reason to maintain the structure. In this view, some change is the price of keeping the past standing.

Based on the texts, how would the advocates of adaptive reuse in Text 2 most likely respond to the preservationists' position in Text 1?
c: They would argue that strict restoration may endanger the very buildings it is meant to protect.
They would agree that any modern alteration leaves a building historic in name only.
They would claim that the original paint colors of old buildings can rarely be identified.
They would argue that old textile mills are less historically important than other kinds of old buildings.
a: Metin 2'ye göre kullanılamayan bina ayakta kalamaz; dolayısıyla katı restorasyon ısrarı, korumak istediği binaların varlığını tehlikeye atabilir.

s:
In traditional Japanese papermaking, fibers from the inner bark of the kozo shrub are first boiled to soften them and then beaten by hand into a loose pulp. The pulp is stirred into a vat of water along with a plant-based thickener that keeps the fibers evenly suspended. ______ the papermaker dips a bamboo screen into the vat and rocks it back and forth so that the fibers interlock in thin, even layers. The wet sheets are then stacked, pressed, and dried on boards.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
a: Parça kâğıt yapımının aşamalarını sırayla anlatır; hamurun hazırlanmasından sonra eleğin daldırılması bir sonraki adımdır, bu yüzden "Next" uygundur.

s:
Few places on Earth receive less rain than parts of Chile's Atacama Desert, where some weather stations have gone years without recording measurable rainfall. The desert's soils are so dry and so poor in organic matter that scientists have used them to test instruments designed to search for life on Mars ______ if a device cannot detect microbes in the Atacama, researchers reason, it is unlikely to succeed on a planet that is even drier.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
a: Boşluğun iki yanında iki bağımsız cümle vardır; bunları noktalı virgül bağlayabilir. Yalnız virgül cümle eklemesi, noktalamasız kullanım ise kaynaşık cümle hatası olur.

s:
Before the mid-nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks by the local position of the sun, so noon in one town might arrive several minutes before noon in a town to its west. For travelers on horseback, such small differences hardly mattered. Railways changed that. A train passing through many towns in a single day could not keep to a schedule written in dozens of local times, and confusion over timetables led to missed connections and raised the risk of accidents. Railway companies therefore adopted shared standard times, and governments gradually followed, turning a scheduling convenience into the time zones still in use today.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To explain how a change in transportation led to the adoption of standardized time
To argue that local solar time was more accurate than the standard time that replaced it
To compare the speed of early trains with the speed of travel on horseback
To describe the role that governments played in building the earliest railways
a: Parça, demiryollarının yerel saatlerle tarife tutmayı imkânsız kılması sonucu standart saatin ve saat dilimlerinin nasıl benimsendiğini açıklar.

s:
Psychologists have found that people often remember information better when they produce it themselves than when they simply read it, a pattern known as the generation effect. For example, a person who completes the clue "opposite of hot: c___" tends to remember the word "cold" better than a person who reads the pair "hot, cold." One research team argues that the benefit arises because generating an answer forces people to think about the meaning of what they are learning.

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the research team's argument?
c: People who generated words by unscrambling letters, without considering meaning, remembered them as well as people who used meaningful clues.
People who generated words from meaningful clues remembered them better than people who simply read the same words printed in a list of word pairs.
People who generated words from meaningful clues took longer to respond than people who only read the completed word pairs.
People who read word pairs aloud remembered them slightly better than people who read the same word pairs silently.

s:
Astronomers can estimate the age of a star cluster by noting which of its stars have left the stable phase of their lives and begun to swell into giants. Because massive stars use up their fuel much faster than smaller stars do, the most massive stars in a cluster are the first to leave the stable phase. In a young cluster, even very massive stars may still be stable, while in an older cluster only relatively small stars remain so. Thus, if all of the stable stars in a cluster are of low mass, astronomers would most likely conclude that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: its massive stars burn fuel slowly.
its giants will soon become stable.

s:
Tardigrades, microscopic animals found in moss, soil, and ocean sediments, are famous for their ability to endure conditions that would kill most other organisms. When their surroundings dry out, they draw in their legs, lose nearly all of their body water, and enter a dormant state in which their metabolism becomes almost undetectable. Researchers have long been puzzled by how tardigrade cells survive such extreme drying, and recent work points to specialized proteins that may form a glassy material inside cells, holding delicate structures in place until water returns.

As used in the text, what does the word "endure" most nearly mean?
a: Tardigradların çoğu canlıyı öldürecek koşullara dayanabildiği anlatıldığından "endure" burada katlanmak, dayanmak anlamındadır.

s:

An analyst reviewing a year of trip data claimed that casual riders' use of the program depends much more heavily on the season than members' use does, perhaps because many casual riders are tourists or people riding for leisure in warm weather. The graph shows the average number of daily trips taken by each group in selected months of that year.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the analyst's claim?
c: From January to July, casual riders' average daily trips rose from 50 to 600, while members' rose from 200 to 500.
In March, members took twice as many average daily trips as casual riders did, at 300 trips compared with 150 trips.

s:

• Some concrete structures built by the ancient Romans, including harbor walls, have stood for roughly two thousand years.

c: Lime lumps in Roman concrete may fill cracks when water seeps in, which could help explain its long life.
Modern concrete often breaks down within decades in seawater, but Roman harbor walls have lasted far longer.

Many of the singers they recorded had never heard their own voices played back. The collection of songs that the researchers gathered during those trips ______ now available to the public through a university's online archive.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

s:
Landscape designers use the term "desire path" for the narrow trail worn into grass when people repeatedly cut across a lawn instead of following paved walkways. Such paths are often treated as a nuisance, and some property managers respond by putting up fences or signs. Other designers see them as free information. At some universities, planners have deliberately waited a season before paving new walkways, then laid pavement along whatever routes students had worn into the grass. The resulting networks, these designers argue, reflect how people actually move rather than how a planner imagined they would.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To describe how some designers use an informal pattern of movement to guide planning decisions
To argue that fences and signs are the most effective ways to protect lawns from damage
To explain why students generally prefer walking on grass to walking on paved walkways
To criticize universities for spending too much money on building and repairing walkways
a: Parça, kendiliğinden oluşan patikaları sorun saymak yerine yürüyüş yollarının yerini belirlemek için kullanan tasarımcıları anlatır.

s:

One explanation is that speakers hear frequent irregular forms so often that they memorize them, whereas rarely heard irregular forms are easily forgotten and replaced by the regular pattern. If this explanation is correct, it would follow that ______

c: an irregular verb that becomes much less common over time is more likely to become regular.
irregular verbs tend to become regular only after they have become very commonly used.
the irregular past tense of "go" is likely to be replaced by a regular form fairly soon.
speakers memorize regular past-tense forms more easily than they memorize irregular ones.

The table shows the average yields in the first and third years of the study.

Plots without a cover crop yielded nearly the same amount of corn in Year 1 as they did in Year 3.

Modern art conservators generally follow a principle of reversibility: any material they add to a damaged painting, from a protective varnish to the filler used in cracks, should be removable by future conservators without harming the original paint. a: Önceki cümleler uykunun hem belleğe hem de beynin bakımına katkısını anlatır; uyku eksikliğinin her ikisini de etkileyebileceği bunlardan çıkan bir sonuçtur, bu yüzden "Thus" uygundur.

Her extensive notes on the article, which were considerably longer than the article ______ included a step-by-step method for calculating a sequence of values known as Bernoulli numbers. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
a: "which were considerably longer than the article itself" araya giren bir yan cümledir ve virgülle açıldığı için virgülle kapanmalıdır; ardından ana fiil "included" gelir.

s:
Projects that invite volunteers to classify galaxies, count birds, or transcribe old weather logs have produced data sets far larger than professional researchers could assemble alone. Skeptics once worried that untrained participants would make too many errors. Project designers responded not by demanding expertise but by building in redundancy: each image or record is reviewed by several volunteers, and their combined judgment is used. According to some evaluations, this consensus has proved roughly as reliable as the judgment of a single expert, while allowing far more material to be examined.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Citizen science projects have eased worries about accuracy by having several volunteers review each item.
Citizen science projects now require volunteers to complete formal training before they classify any data.
Professional researchers have largely stopped relying on expert judgment when they classify scientific data.
Skeptics have shown that volunteers make more errors than trained experts do in most citizen science projects.
a: Parçanın odağı, gönüllülerin hata yapacağı kaygısına her kaydın birden çok gönüllüce incelenmesiyle (yedeklilik) yanıt verilmesidir.

Fireflies produce their flashes through a chemical reaction that takes place in specialized light organs near the end of the abdomen. Oxygen supplied through tiny air tubes allows the insects to switch the reaction on and off, creating the patterns that different species use to attract mates. The reaction, which involves a compound called luciferin, ______ very little of its energy as heat, which is why firefly light is often described as "cold light."

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
a: Cümlenin öznesi "The reaction"dır ve araya giren yan cümleden sonra çekimli bir ana fiil gerekir; diğer biçimler çekimsiz olduğu için cümle yüklemsiz kalır.

s:
Most land plants do not absorb nutrients from the soil entirely on their own. Their roots are typically colonized by mycorrhizal fungi, organisms that form a mutually beneficial partnership with the plant. The fungus extends a dense network of microscopic threads, called hyphae, far beyond the zone that the roots themselves can reach. Because these threads are much thinner than even the finest root hairs, they can penetrate tiny pores in the soil and extract water and mineral nutrients, especially phosphorus, that would otherwise remain inaccessible. In return, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis, a payment that some researchers estimate can amount to a significant share of the plant's carbon budget.

The relationship is ancient. Fossilized remains of some of the earliest land plants show structures strikingly similar to those of modern mycorrhizae. This evidence has led many biologists to propose that the partnership was not merely a later refinement but a precondition for the colonization of land. Early plants lacked true roots, and the rocky, nutrient-poor surfaces they encountered would have offered little sustenance without fungal assistance.

The partnership is not, however, uniformly cooperative. Under conditions in which nutrients are abundant, plants may reduce the amount of carbon they allocate to their fungal partners, and in some cases the fungus appears to deliver fewer nutrients than it receives in sugar. Such observations suggest that the relationship is better understood as a continuous negotiation than as a fixed exchange. Indeed, experiments indicate that some plants can preferentially reward the fungal strains that supply the most phosphorus, a form of biological market in which cooperation is sustained because uncooperative partners are penalized.

The word "sustenance" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: “Sustenance” besin, beslenme demektir; parçada ilk bitkilerin besince fakir kayalık yüzeylerde mantar yardımı olmadan yeterli besin bulamayacağı anlatılır.

The partnership is not, however, uniformly cooperative. Under conditions in which nutrients are abundant, plants may reduce the amount of carbon they allocate to their fungal partners, and in some cases the fungus appears to deliver fewer nutrients than it receives in sugar. Such observations suggest that the relationship is better understood as a continuous negotiation than as a fixed exchange. Indeed, experiments indicate that some plants can preferentially reward the fungal strains that supply the most phosphorus, a form of biological market in which cooperation is sustained because uncooperative partners are penalized.

Karst is the name geologists give to landscapes shaped largely by the dissolution of soluble rock, most commonly limestone. Limestone consists mainly of calcium carbonate, a mineral that is only slightly soluble in pure water. Rainwater, however, is rarely pure. As it falls through the atmosphere and then percolates through soil rich in decaying organic matter, it absorbs carbon dioxide and becomes a weak carbonic acid. When this mildly acidic water seeps into cracks in the bedrock, it slowly dissolves the surrounding stone, widening fractures into channels and, over tens of thousands of years, into extensive cave systems.

The surface expression of this process is distinctive. Because water drains rapidly downward through the rock rather than flowing across it, karst regions often have few permanent streams. Rivers may vanish abruptly into openings in the ground, travel underground for considerable distances, and reemerge as springs. Sinkholes, which are circular depressions formed when the roof of an underground cavity collapses or when the surface gradually subsides into dissolved rock below, may dot the land by the thousands.

Karst terrain poses particular challenges for human communities. Since the underground passages connect directly to the surface, pollutants spilled on the ground can enter aquifers with little natural filtering and travel quickly over long distances. Contaminants that would be trapped and broken down in the fine pores of sandy soil may instead pass almost unchanged into drinking-water supplies. Furthermore, the sudden formation of sinkholes can damage roads and buildings, and excessive pumping of groundwater may accelerate collapse by removing the water that once helped support the roofs of cavities. For these reasons, planners in karst regions increasingly rely on detailed mapping of subsurface features before approving new construction.

It contains calcium carbonate collected from the soil.
It freezes in cracks and splits the rock into pieces.

During the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, a series of trade fairs held in the county of Champagne, in what is now northeastern France, became a principal meeting place for merchants from across Europe. Italian traders arrived with spices, silks, and other goods imported from the eastern Mediterranean, while merchants from Flanders brought the fine woolen cloth for which their region was famous. The fairs rotated among several towns according to a fixed calendar, so that one or another was in session for much of the year.

The success of the fairs owed a great deal to the policies of the counts who ruled Champagne. Rather than treating passing merchants as a convenient source of tolls to be squeezed, the counts guaranteed their safety on the roads leading to the fairs and appointed officials to keep order and to settle disputes. These officials enforced contracts impartially, regardless of a merchant's origin, which gave foreign traders the confidence to do business with strangers.

Over time, the fairs evolved from places where goods physically changed hands into centers of finance. Because so many merchants gathered at predictable times, debts incurred at one fair could be settled at the next, and written instruments promising payment came to substitute for the transport of coins, which was both cumbersome and dangerous. In this sense, the fairs functioned as an early clearinghouse.

Their prominence did not last. By the early fourteenth century, Italian merchants had begun sending ships directly to the ports of Flanders, bypassing the overland route through Champagne. At the same time, political changes in the region brought heavier taxation and less reliable protection. Merchants who no longer needed to travel in person increasingly preferred to conduct business through permanent agents stationed in major commercial cities.

c: The fairs moved among several towns according to a set schedule.
Each town held a single fair that lasted for most of the year.
Italian merchants demanded that the markets remain open constantly.
Flemish cloth was produced continuously and needed a steady outlet.

Fresco, the technique of painting on freshly applied plaster, was the dominant method of mural decoration in Italy from the late thirteenth through the sixteenth century. In its purest form, known as buon fresco, pigments ground in water are brushed onto a layer of wet lime plaster. As the plaster dries, it reacts with carbon dioxide in the air to form a thin crystalline skin of calcium carbonate that binds the pigment particles within the wall itself. The result is remarkably durable: properly executed frescoes can survive for centuries, provided they are protected from persistent moisture.

The chemistry of the method imposed strict demands on the painter. Because the plaster remained receptive to pigment for only a matter of hours, an artist could apply only as much fresh plaster as could be painted in a single working session. Each such section, called a giornata, from the Italian word for "day," was joined to its neighbors along seams that conservators can often still detect. Studying the shape and sequence of these patches allows scholars to reconstruct the order in which a large composition was painted and, occasionally, to estimate how long the project took.

The technique also limited the painter's palette. Certain pigments, including some vivid blues and greens, either reacted badly with lime or could not be bound effectively by it. These colors had to be applied afterward on dry plaster, a method called fresco secco, using a binding agent such as egg or glue. Such additions are far less stable, which is why the areas painted a secco in many old murals have flaked away, leaving faded or blank patches in places where the original design called for the richest colors.

c: A crystalline layer that forms as the plaster reacts with air
A binding agent, such as egg, that the painter mixes into the paint
A coat of glue applied over the surface after painting
Water in which the pigments were ground before painting

s:
Red dwarfs are the most common type of star in the Milky Way, accounting by many estimates for roughly three-quarters of the stars in our galactic neighborhood. They are smaller, cooler, and far dimmer than the Sun, and they consume their hydrogen fuel so slowly that their lifetimes are expected to exceed the current age of the universe many times over. For astronomers searching for potentially habitable planets, these characteristics present both an opportunity and a problem.

The opportunity lies partly in observation. Because a red dwarf is faint, its habitable zone, the range of orbital distances at which liquid water could exist on a planet's surface, lies very close to the star. A planet orbiting within that zone completes an orbit in a matter of days or weeks, and when it passes in front of its small host star, it blocks a relatively large fraction of the starlight. Both factors make such planets easier to detect than Earth-like planets orbiting Sun-like stars.

The same proximity, however, creates difficulties. A planet that close is likely to become tidally locked, meaning that one hemisphere permanently faces the star while the other remains in perpetual darkness. Some early models predicted that the atmosphere of such a world would freeze out on the cold night side. More recent simulations suggest that a sufficiently thick atmosphere could circulate heat effectively enough to prevent this. A more serious concern is stellar activity. Young red dwarfs in particular emit frequent, powerful flares of ultraviolet and X-ray radiation, which could gradually strip away a nearby planet's atmosphere. Whether planets in these systems can retain the air and water that life as we know it requires remains one of the central open questions in the field.

According to paragraph 1, which of the following is true of red dwarfs?
c: They use their fuel so slowly that they will shine for an extremely long time.
They are hotter than the Sun, although they are much smaller and fainter in appearance.
They make up a small but growing fraction of the stars in the Milky Way.
They are expected to burn out before the universe reaches twice its age.

s:
One of the most robust findings in the psychology of memory is the spacing effect: information studied in several sessions separated by intervals is generally retained far longer than the same information studied for an equal total time in a single concentrated session. The phenomenon was documented in the late nineteenth century, and it has since been replicated with learners of many ages and with materials ranging from vocabulary lists to motor skills.

Several explanations have been proposed. According to one account, when material is repeated immediately, it still feels familiar, so the learner processes it superficially. When the repetition is delayed, by contrast, the learner must work to retrieve the material from memory, and this effortful retrieval appears to strengthen the memory trace. A second account emphasizes context. Each study session takes place in a slightly different mental and physical setting, so spaced study links the material to a wider variety of cues that can later help to bring it to mind.

Despite the strength of the evidence, the spacing effect is underused. Students commonly prefer to cram, and their preference is understandable. Massed study often produces better performance on a test given immediately afterward, and the fluency learners experience while rereading recently studied material creates a convincing but misleading sense of mastery. Spaced practice, in contrast, feels harder and less productive in the moment precisely because some forgetting has occurred between sessions. Researchers sometimes describe such conditions as "desirable difficulties": obstacles that slow apparent progress during learning yet enhance long-term retention. The challenge for educators, therefore, is not only to schedule review sessions at intervals but also to persuade learners that the sense of struggle is a sign of effective study rather than of failure.

The word "robust" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: “Robust” burada sağlam, iyi kanıtlanmış anlamındadır; parçada bulgunun on dokuzuncu yüzyıldan beri pek çok yaş grubu ve materyalle tekrarlandığı belirtilir.

s:
Each year, billions of birds undertake migrations that may span thousands of kilometers, often returning with remarkable precision to the same breeding sites. How they find their way has long fascinated biologists, and research over the past several decades indicates that birds do not rely on a single navigational aid but integrate information from several sources.

The sun is one of the most important. Birds can determine direction from the sun's position, but because that position shifts across the sky during the day, using it accurately requires compensating for the time. Experiments in which birds' internal clocks were shifted by several hours, by exposing them to artificial cycles of light and darkness, showed that the birds subsequently oriented in predictably wrong directions. This result indicated that they were combining the sun's position with an internal sense of time.

Many species migrate at night, however, and these birds use the stars. Young birds raised under an artificial planetarium sky learned to treat the point around which the projected stars appeared to rotate as north, even when that point was deliberately placed elsewhere. Rather than inheriting a fixed map of particular constellations, then, they seem to learn the center of celestial rotation during development.

In addition, birds are sensitive to the Earth's magnetic field. Some evidence suggests that they perceive it through specialized molecules in the eye, whereas other findings point to receptors in the region of the beak, although their exact nature is still debated. The two mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, and it is possible that they serve different functions, one providing a compass direction and the other information about location. When cues conflict, birds appear to recalibrate one system against another, a flexibility that may help them cope with cloud cover, seasonal changes, and local magnetic irregularities.

The word "integrate" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: “Integrate” birleştirmek demektir; parçada kuşların tek bir yardımcıya değil, birden çok kaynaktan gelen bilgiyi bir araya getirmeye dayandığı anlatılır.

Cities are often warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. The difference is most pronounced not during the hottest part of the day but at night, when a city may remain several degrees warmer than nearby rural areas.

Several features of urban environments contribute to this effect. Materials such as asphalt, concrete, and brick absorb large amounts of solar energy during the day and release it slowly after sunset. In addition, cities contain little vegetation. Plants and moist soil cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration, the process by which water evaporates from soil and from the leaves of plants, consuming heat as it does so. Replacing fields and forests with impermeable surfaces, which shed rainwater into drains rather than retaining it, removes much of this natural cooling. The geometry of the city also matters. Tall buildings lining narrow streets trap heat radiated from the ground that would otherwise escape to the night sky, and they reduce the wind that might carry warm air away. Finally, vehicles, air conditioners, and industry add heat directly.

The consequences extend beyond discomfort. Elevated nighttime temperatures deny residents relief during heat waves, and public health researchers have linked prolonged exposure to such conditions with increased illness, particularly among the elderly. Higher temperatures also raise demand for air conditioning, which consumes electricity and releases still more waste heat.

Cities have begun experimenting with countermeasures. Roofs and pavements coated with reflective materials absorb less sunlight, and planting trees provides both shade and evaporative cooling. Green roofs, covered with a layer of soil and vegetation, can lower the temperature of the buildings beneath them. The effectiveness of each strategy depends on local climate, however; measures that rely on evaporation may work well in a dry climate but offer less benefit where the air is already humid.

The placebo effect, in which patients improve after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient, has long been treated by medical researchers as a nuisance to be controlled for rather than a phenomenon worth studying. In clinical trials, a new drug is considered effective only if it performs better than a sugar pill, and any improvement in the placebo group is usually dismissed as noise. In recent decades, however, a growing number of scientists have begun to examine the effect in its own right. Their work suggests that placebo responses are not simply imaginary. Brain imaging studies have shown, for example, that the expectation of pain relief can trigger the release of the body's own pain-reducing chemicals. The strength of the response also appears to depend on context: expensive-looking pills, injections and confident doctors tend to produce larger effects than cheap tablets handed over without explanation. Perhaps most surprisingly, some studies report that patients may benefit even when they are told openly that the pill they are taking contains no medicine. These findings do not mean that placebos can cure serious diseases such as cancer, and researchers stress that the effect is strongest for subjective symptoms like pain, nausea and fatigue. Nevertheless, they raise an important question for medicine: if the way a treatment is delivered influences how well it works, then the doctor's manner and the setting of care may deserve more attention than they currently receive.

a: “Nuisance” sıkıntı, baş belası demektir; araştırmacılar plasebo etkisini incelenecek bir olgu değil, denetlenmesi gereken bir sıkıntı olarak görmüştür. En yakın anlam “annoyance”.

When Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable metal type in Mainz around 1450, he could hardly have foreseen how quickly the technology would spread. Within roughly fifty years, printing presses were operating in more than two hundred European towns, and millions of books had been produced. Historians have long debated the consequences of this transformation. One traditional view holds that printing led directly to mass literacy, but this claim is difficult to sustain. Books remained expensive for decades, and in most regions the majority of the population still could not read well into the eighteenth century. What printing did change, almost immediately, was the speed and uniformity with which ideas circulated among those who were already literate. Before print, a text copied by hand could differ significantly from one copy to the next, as scribes introduced errors or made deliberate changes. Printed editions, by contrast, allowed scholars in different cities to refer to the same page of the same text, which made it far easier to compare, criticise and build upon one another's work. Some historians argue that this shared reference point was a precondition for the rapid scientific exchanges of later centuries. Printing also played a decisive role in religious and political debates, since pamphlets could be produced cheaply and distributed widely within weeks. In this sense, the press may have transformed public life less by teaching people to read than by changing what readers could do with texts.

a: “This claim is difficult to sustain” cümlesinde “sustain” bir iddiayı savunmak, ayakta tutmak anlamındadır; en yakın anlam “defend”.

Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support an extraordinary share of marine life, providing food and shelter for roughly a quarter of all known marine species. The corals that build these reefs live in a close partnership with tiny algae that inhabit their tissues. The algae produce food through photosynthesis and pass much of it to the coral, while also giving reefs their bright colours. This relationship, however, is sensitive to temperature. When the water becomes unusually warm for several weeks, the partnership breaks down and the corals expel the algae, leaving their white skeletons visible through transparent tissue. This process, known as bleaching, does not kill corals immediately, but without their algae they are starved of most of their energy. If temperatures return to normal quickly, corals can regain their algae and recover; if the heat lasts too long, large areas of reef may die. Scientists have recorded several mass bleaching events across the world's tropical oceans in recent decades, and they warn that such events are becoming more frequent as sea temperatures rise. A reef that bleaches every two or three years may never have enough time to recover fully. Efforts to protect reefs therefore include reducing local pressures such as pollution and overfishing, which can make corals more resilient, as well as experimental projects to breed corals that tolerate heat better.

s:
Classical economic theory assumed that people make decisions by weighing costs and benefits in a consistent way. If losing a hundred dollars makes someone exactly as unhappy as gaining a hundred dollars makes them happy, then their choices should be predictable and stable. Beginning in the 1970s, however, the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed through a series of experiments that real human behaviour departs from this model in systematic ways. One of their best-known findings is loss aversion: for most people, the pain of losing something is considerably stronger than the pleasure of gaining something of equal value. As a result, people will often reject a bet that offers an even chance of winning or losing the same amount of money, even though, on average, they would lose nothing by accepting it. Loss aversion also helps to explain why investors tend to hold on to falling shares for too long, hoping to avoid admitting a loss, and why people value objects they own more highly than identical objects they do not own. Such findings contributed to the rise of behavioural economics, a field that combines insights from psychology with economic analysis. Critics have pointed out that the size of loss aversion varies between studies and situations, and that some laboratory results may not hold in real markets. Even so, the idea that losses loom larger than gains is now widely accepted as an important feature of human decision-making.

The word "systematic" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: İnsan davranışının modelden “systematic ways” ile sapması, rastgele değil tutarlı ve öngörülebilir biçimlerde saptığını anlatır; en yakın anlam “consistent and predictable”.

Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, a large proportion are considered endangered, and linguists estimate that many of them may stop being spoken within this century. A language rarely disappears because its speakers suddenly abandon it. More often, the process is gradual: parents who speak a minority language begin to raise their children in a more widely used language, believing that it will offer them better opportunities in education and employment. The children may still understand the language of their grandparents, but they rarely use it, and their own children may not learn it at all. When the last fluent speakers die, the language disappears with them, together with knowledge that may not exist anywhere else, such as names for local plants, traditional stories and ways of describing the world. In response, communities and researchers have developed a range of revitalisation efforts. These include recording elderly speakers, producing dictionaries and teaching materials, and creating schools in which children are taught through the endangered language. Some projects have been remarkably successful. Hebrew, for instance, which for centuries was used mainly in religious and written contexts, became the everyday language of millions of people in the twentieth century. Such cases are exceptional, however, and most experts agree that revival is possible only when a community itself is strongly committed to using the language in daily life.

The word "revitalisation" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: “Revitalisation efforts” dili yeniden canlandırma çabalarıdır; en yakın anlam “renewal” (yenilenme, canlanma).

The discovery of antibiotics in the twentieth century transformed medicine, turning infections that had once been fatal into conditions that could be treated within days. Almost from the beginning, however, scientists warned that bacteria would fight back. Because bacteria reproduce very rapidly, random genetic changes appear frequently in large populations. When an antibiotic is used, it kills the bacteria that are sensitive to it, but any that happen to carry a change allowing them to survive are left to multiply. Over time, the resistant strain can become dominant. Bacteria can also pass genes for resistance directly to one another, sometimes even between different species, which allows resistance to spread faster than mutation alone would permit. Human behaviour has accelerated this natural process. Antibiotics are often prescribed for viral illnesses such as colds, against which they have no effect, and patients sometimes stop taking their medicine as soon as they feel better, allowing the hardiest bacteria to survive. In many countries, large quantities of antibiotics are also given to farm animals to promote growth or prevent disease. Health organisations now describe antimicrobial resistance as one of the most serious threats to global health, since routine operations and treatments such as chemotherapy depend on the ability to prevent and treat infections. Meanwhile, relatively few new classes of antibiotics have been developed in recent decades, partly because such drugs are less profitable for pharmaceutical companies than medicines that patients take for many years.

a: Hastalar ilacı erken bırakınca “the hardiest bacteria”, yani en dayanıklı, hayatta kalma yeteneği en yüksek bakteriler yaşamaya devam eder.

When large numbers of office workers began working from home, managers and researchers were eager to know whether productivity would rise or fall. The evidence so far suggests that there is no simple answer. Several studies have found that employees working remotely complete as much work as their colleagues in the office, or even more, partly because they spend less time commuting and are interrupted less often. Other research, however, points to costs that are harder to measure. Workers at home tend to communicate mainly with people they already know well, and they have fewer of the informal conversations through which new ideas often emerge. Younger employees may also find it harder to learn from experienced colleagues when they cannot observe them at work. The type of task appears to matter a great deal. Work that requires long periods of concentration, such as writing a report or analysing data, often benefits from the quiet of a home office, while tasks that depend on close collaboration or creative brainstorming may suffer. For this reason, many organisations have settled on hybrid arrangements, in which employees spend some days in the office and others at home. Supporters argue that this combines the advantages of both, although critics note that it can also combine their disadvantages if teams do not coordinate which days they come in, so that people travel to the office only to spend the day on video calls.

The phrase "settled on" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: “Many organisations have settled on hybrid arrangements” cümlesinde “settle on” bir seçenekte karar kılmak demektir; en yakın anlam “decided to adopt”.

In April 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted in what is considered the most powerful volcanic eruption in recorded history. Tens of thousands of people on the island and nearby areas died, either directly or from the famine and disease that followed. The effects, however, extended far beyond the region. The eruption threw enormous amounts of sulphur gas high into the atmosphere, where it formed a fine layer of particles that reflected part of the sun's light back into space. Over the following year, average temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere fell noticeably. In 1816, which became known in Europe and North America as the "Year Without a Summer", snow fell in parts of New England in June, and cold, wet weather destroyed crops across much of Western Europe. Food prices rose sharply, and hunger contributed to social unrest and migration. Interestingly, people at the time had little idea that these disasters were connected to an eruption on the other side of the world; the link was established by scientists much later. The episode is now frequently studied by climate researchers, because it shows how quickly a change in the composition of the atmosphere can affect weather and food supplies on a global scale. It has also been cited in discussions of proposals to cool the planet artificially by releasing particles into the upper atmosphere, a strategy whose risks remain highly controversial.

The word "unrest" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: Gıda fiyatları yükselince açlık “social unrest”e, yani toplumsal huzursuzluk ve kargaşaya katkıda bulundu; en yakın anlam “disorder”.

For much of the twentieth century, raising children with two languages was widely believed to be harmful. Educators and some psychologists warned that bilingual children would become confused, fall behind in school, or fail to master either language properly. Later research largely overturned this view. Studies found that bilingual children may know fewer words in each individual language than monolingual children of the same age, but that their total vocabulary across both languages is usually similar, and that any delay in one language tends to disappear over time. More controversially, some researchers proposed that bilingualism brings cognitive advantages. Because bilingual people must constantly keep one language active while suppressing the other, they argued, they develop stronger executive control, the set of mental skills used to focus attention and switch between tasks. Early experiments appeared to support this claim, and it received considerable attention in the media. In recent years, however, several large studies have failed to find consistent differences between bilingual and monolingual participants on such tasks, and some researchers suspect that studies reporting an advantage were more likely to be published than those that did not. The debate is far from settled. What is clear, according to most specialists, is that bilingualism does not harm children's development, and that its practical benefits, such as the ability to communicate with more people and access different cultures, are reason enough to value it.

a: “Later research largely overturned this view” cümlesinde “overturn” bir görüşü çürütüp tersine çevirmektir; en yakın anlam “reversed”.

Honeybees are often presented as the most important pollinators of crops, and in many farming systems they do play a central role. Large numbers of hives are transported from farm to farm to pollinate fruit trees and other crops during their short flowering seasons. However, ecologists increasingly emphasise that wild insects, including thousands of species of solitary bees, bumblebees, hoverflies and beetles, are also essential. Some studies have found that wild pollinators improve the quantity and quality of fruit even on farms where honeybees are abundant, apparently because different insects visit flowers at different times of day, in different weather conditions, or in different ways. Bumblebees, for example, can fly in cooler and windier weather than honeybees, and some plants release their pollen only when a flower is vibrated by a buzzing insect, a technique honeybees do not use. Unlike honeybees, which are managed by beekeepers, wild pollinators depend entirely on the surrounding landscape for food and nesting sites. Intensive agriculture, the loss of hedges and wildflower meadows, and the use of certain pesticides have all contributed to declines in many wild species. Interest in urban beekeeping has grown in many cities, and while this can raise public awareness, some researchers warn that adding large numbers of honeybee hives to small green areas may increase competition for flowers and leave less food for wild bees. Protecting pollination, they argue, depends more on planting diverse flowers and preserving habitats than on keeping more hives.

The word "abundant" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: “Even on farms where honeybees are abundant” bal arılarının bol olduğu çiftlikleri anlatır; en yakın anlam “plentiful”.

Parents of teenagers often complain that their children stay up late and are almost impossible to wake in the morning. It is tempting to blame this on laziness or on the attractions of mobile phones, but research suggests that biology plays a significant role. During puberty, the body's internal clock shifts, so that the hormone melatonin, which helps to bring on sleep, is released later in the evening than in childhood. As a result, many adolescents simply do not feel sleepy until late at night. Their need for sleep, however, does not decrease; most experts recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night. When school starts early, many of them are forced to get up long before their bodies are ready, and they accumulate a significant sleep debt over the week. This has been linked to poorer concentration, lower academic performance, mood problems and an increased risk of accidents among young drivers. Several school districts that have experimented with later start times have reported that students sleep longer, attend classes more regularly and are less likely to fall asleep in lessons. Changing school schedules is not simple, though, since it affects transport, parents' working hours and after-school activities. Screens and evening habits also matter: bright light from devices late at night can delay sleep further, which is why researchers recommend combining later start times with better sleep habits at home.

s:
Parents of teenagers often complain that their children stay up late and are almost impossible to wake in the morning. It is tempting to blame this on laziness or on the attractions of mobile phones, but research suggests that biology plays a significant role. During puberty, the body's internal clock shifts, so that the hormone melatonin, which helps to bring on sleep, is released later in the evening than in childhood. As a result, many adolescents simply do not feel sleepy until late at night. Their need for sleep, however, does not decrease; most experts recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night. When school starts early, many of them are forced to get up long before their bodies are ready, and they accumulate a significant sleep debt over the week. This has been linked to poorer concentration, lower academic performance, mood problems and an increased risk of accidents among young drivers. Several school districts that have experimented with later start times have reported that students sleep longer, attend classes more regularly and are less likely to fall asleep in lessons. Changing school schedules is not simple, though, since it affects transport, parents' working hours and after-school activities. Screens and evening habits also matter: bright light from devices late at night can delay sleep further, which is why researchers recommend combining later start times with better sleep habits at home.

According to the passage, how much sleep do most experts recommend for teenagers?
c: Between eight and ten hours a night
About six hours on school nights
As much as adults need, around seven hours

Plastic does not biodegrade in the way that wood or paper does. Instead, exposure to sunlight, waves and changes in temperature gradually breaks larger items into smaller and smaller fragments. Pieces smaller than five millimetres are usually described as microplastics, and they are now found almost everywhere scientists look: in deep ocean sediments, Arctic ice, agricultural soils, drinking water and the air of cities. Some microplastics are produced deliberately at a small size, such as the tiny beads once commonly added to cosmetics, but most result from the breakdown of bottles, bags, fishing nets and synthetic clothing, which releases fibres when it is washed. Because microplastics are so small, they can be eaten by plankton and other small organisms at the base of the food chain, and they have been detected in fish, shellfish and, increasingly, in human tissues. What remains uncertain is how harmful they are. Laboratory studies have shown that high concentrations can damage the health of some marine animals, and that plastic particles can carry chemicals added during manufacturing or absorbed from the environment. For humans, however, the evidence is still limited, partly because measuring very small particles accurately is technically difficult and because people are exposed to many other substances at the same time. Scientists therefore call for more research, while many argue that, given how persistent plastic is, it would be sensible to reduce plastic pollution without waiting for definitive proof of harm.

The word "persistent" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: Son cümlede plastiğin ne kadar “persistent” olduğu, yani çevrede ne kadar uzun süre kalıcı olduğu vurgulanır; en yakın anlam “long-lasting”.

The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast network of overland and sea routes that connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe for well over a thousand years. Few merchants ever travelled its entire length. Instead, goods usually passed from one trader to another, changing hands many times in the markets and caravan stops along the way. Chinese silk, which gave the network its name in the nineteenth century, was certainly an important product, but the routes also carried spices, precious metals, glassware, horses, paper and countless other items. Equally significant was the exchange of ideas and technologies. Buddhism travelled from India into Central Asia and China along these routes, and later Islam spread eastward through the same networks. Techniques for making paper moved westward from China, eventually reaching the Islamic world and then Europe, where they contributed to profound changes in the recording and spread of knowledge. Not everything that travelled was beneficial, however. Historians believe that the plague known as the Black Death, which killed a large proportion of Europe's population in the fourteenth century, spread partly along trade routes connecting Asia and Europe. The history of the Silk Road is therefore often used to illustrate a broader point: that long-distance connections between societies bring both opportunities and risks, a lesson that seems highly relevant in today's globalised world.

s:
The human digestive system is home to trillions of microorganisms, most of them bacteria, which together are known as the gut microbiome. For a long time these microbes received little attention, apart from the few that cause disease. Advances in genetic sequencing, however, have made it possible to identify thousands of species that cannot easily be grown in a laboratory, and research into the microbiome has expanded dramatically. It is now clear that gut bacteria perform many useful functions. They help to break down dietary fibre that human enzymes cannot digest, producing substances that nourish the cells lining the intestine; they produce certain vitamins; and they appear to play a role in training the immune system. Differences in the composition of the microbiome have been associated with a wide range of conditions, including obesity, inflammatory bowel disease and even some mental health problems. Such findings have generated great excitement, and the market for probiotic supplements has grown accordingly. Many scientists, however, urge caution. Most of the studies show associations rather than causes: it is often unclear whether a particular microbiome contributes to a disease or is simply a consequence of it. Moreover, the microbiome varies greatly from person to person, which makes it difficult to define what a healthy one looks like. Diet appears to be one of the strongest influences, and a varied diet rich in fibre is generally considered beneficial, but claims that specific products can reliably improve health should be treated with scepticism.

The word "scepticism" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: Belirli ürünlerin sağlığı iyileştirdiği iddialarına “scepticism” ile, yani şüpheyle yaklaşılması gerektiği söylenir; en yakın anlam “doubt”.

s:
In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner tested an idea that had circulated among country people for some time: that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, seemed to be protected from smallpox, one of the deadliest diseases of the age. Jenner took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and introduced it into a scratch on the arm of a young boy. Some weeks later he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy did not become ill. Experiments of this kind would be considered deeply unethical today, but Jenner's work laid the foundation for vaccination; the word itself comes from vacca, the Latin for cow. The practice spread quickly across Europe and beyond, although it also met strong resistance. Some critics objected on religious grounds, others feared that being injected with material from animals would cause strange side effects, and cartoons of the time showed vaccinated people growing cow-like features. Over the following century and a half, vaccination campaigns gradually reduced smallpox in many countries. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched an intensified global programme to eliminate the disease, relying on careful surveillance and the vaccination of everyone around each new case. The last naturally occurring case was recorded in 1977, and in 1980 smallpox was officially declared eradicated, the first human disease to be eliminated in this way.

The word "eradicated" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: 1980'de çiçek hastalığı resmen “eradicated” ilan edildi; yani tamamen ortadan kaldırıldı. En yakın anlam “completely eliminated”.

s:
Is false information spread more widely online than true information? A large study published in 2018 attempted to answer this question by analysing more than a hundred thousand news stories that had been shared on Twitter over roughly a decade and had been checked by independent fact-checking organisations. The researchers found that false stories reached more people, and did so faster, than true ones. Perhaps surprisingly, automated accounts, or bots, did not explain the difference: when bot activity was removed from the analysis, false news still spread further, suggesting that human users were largely responsible. The authors proposed that novelty may be part of the explanation. False stories tended to be more surprising than true ones, and people may be more inclined to share information that seems new, partly because doing so makes them appear well informed. Replies to false stories also expressed more surprise and disgust, emotions that may encourage sharing. The study has been widely cited, although other researchers have noted that its findings apply to stories that were checked by fact-checkers, which may not be representative of all the news people encounter. Nevertheless, the results have influenced discussions about how platforms and users might respond to misinformation. Some proposals focus on removing false content, while others emphasise simple measures that encourage people to consider whether a story is accurate before they share it.

The word "inclined" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: İnsanların yeni görünen bilgiyi paylaşmaya “more inclined”, yani daha meyilli ve daha olası olabileceği söylenir; en yakın anlam “likely”.

s:
Mountain glaciers are sometimes described as natural water towers. During cold seasons they store water as ice, and during warm, dry months they release it gradually as meltwater, feeding rivers on which millions of people depend for drinking water, farming and electricity. In parts of Asia and South America in particular, glacier melt can make up a significant share of river flow in late summer, when rain is scarce. Most of the world's mountain glaciers are now shrinking as temperatures rise. In the short term, this can actually increase the amount of water flowing in rivers, because more ice is melting each year than before. Scientists warn, however, that this increase is temporary. As glaciers become smaller, the amount of meltwater they can provide eventually reaches a peak and then declines, a point sometimes called "peak water". Some smaller glaciers have probably already passed this point. For communities downstream, the consequences could be serious, particularly in dry seasons, when glacier melt has traditionally helped to maintain river levels. Retreating glaciers can also create hazards, such as lakes held back by unstable piles of rock and ice, which may burst suddenly and cause floods. Adapting to these changes may require new reservoirs, more efficient irrigation and careful planning of water use, measures that are costly and that must often be coordinated between countries sharing the same rivers.

The word "scarce" in the passage is closest in meaning to
a: Yaz sonunda yağmurun “scarce”, yani az ve yetersiz olduğu dönemde buzul erimesinin önemli olduğu söylenir; en yakın anlam “in short supply”.
